source.title: Written in Trade Today
source.summary: Series finale: five Arabic words, five centuries, five lessons for the trade wars of 2025.
source.author: Islamic Economics
source.body_text: In this series finale, we return to the present moment. As tariff walls rise and supply chains fragment, what would a medieval Karimi merchant say about the trade wars of 2025? Five words. Five lessons: transparency works, credit needs trust, maritime freedom benefits all, infrastructure is a public good, and risk should be shared. The principles hidden in our vocabulary are whispering. Are we listening?

thread: A medieval merchant could cash a cheque in Canton using paper written in Baghdad. Modern trade wars forget what those Arabic words knew: credit flows where trust exists.
The Karimi merchants moved goods from Alexandria to Delhi without banks or governments backing them. They had something better: a shared language of commerce that crossed every border.
Tariff means 'notification' in Arabic. It was meant to inform traders, not stop them. We turned transparency into a weapon.

Five Arabic words built global trade. Five lessons for 2025: transparency works, credit needs trust, maritime freedom benefits all, infrastructure serves everyone, risk gets shared. Listen: https://islamiceconomics.github.io/podcast.html#ep-tt-6

linkedin.post: Medieval merchants could cash a cheque in Canton using paper from Baghdad. No central banks. No government guarantees. Just trust encoded in Arabic words that built global trade. The Karimi merchants moved goods from Alexandria to Delhi on reputation alone. They created a vocabulary of commerce that crossed every border: tariff (notification), cheque (written order), magazine (storehouse), admiral (commander of waters). As supply chains fragment in 2025, those five Arabic words whisper five lessons: transparency works better than walls, credit needs trust more than regulation, maritime freedom benefits everyone, infrastructure serves the common good, and risk works best when shared. The principles are still there, written in the words we use every day. Listen: https://islamiceconomics.github.io/podcast.html#ep-tt-6

short_video.voiceover: A merchant in Baghdad writes a cheque. A trader in Canton, four thousand miles away, cashes it immediately. No banks. No government backing. Just five Arabic words that built the first global economy. Tariff meant notification, not barrier. Cheque meant trust across impossible distances. Magazine meant shared infrastructure. Admiral meant protecting trade routes for everyone. Risk meant partnership, not isolation. These principles are still whispering in our vocabulary. As trade wars rise in twenty twenty-five, maybe it's time we listened to what medieval merchants knew about moving goods across borders.
